Poaching Pandemic

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
African wildlife is in deep trouble as the global pandemic has led to another - a poaching pandemic

Unique Selling Point:
Interviews with Derek and Beverly Joubert and unique footage from other african countries

Summary:
In March last year when the world locked down, National Geographic conservationists Beverley and Derek Joubert looked around. They had 660 people working on their Great Plains Safari company in Botswana and absolutely no guests. The 50 billion dollars of revenue that comes into Africa and supports her wildlife dried up overnight and they knew that African wildlife was about to be in deep, deep trouble.

Determined to try and keep their staff, the Joubert’s who have 1.2 million hectares under their custodianship -turned chefs and cooks into instant rangers and managed to keep their staff employed and most of their wildlife safe. But the Joubert’s have never been the kind of people to only consider their own needs, and driven by their imperative to conserve African wildlife, they asked how they could help.

They spoke to conservationists across Africa, and to their network of wildlife investigators and realized another pandemic was taking place as rangers were furloughed, and organised trans national wildlife criminals moved into the vacuum left behind by the rangers.

Says Derek Joubert: “The poaching that is taking place right now is not going to get meat locally – its organised transnational crime. If you consider that there are a billion containers moving around the ocean and about 10% of those have illegal wildlife products in them, so there is an entire industry around this, worth about 27 billion dollars. So the final point of this cycle is that wildlife is collapsing so we are into a second pandemic, a poaching pandemic. The world’s attention and certainly South Africa’s attention needs to focus on keeping rangers employed. It’s our collective duty, and if we don’t do anything, it’s our collective shame,” he says.


Further information:
The examples the Joubert’s give, paint a grim picture. In Tanzania all the rangers were taken out of the field for 8 months leaving wildlife at the mercy of poachers. In Kenya the government is funding a survey that will soon go into the field to see how much wildlife they still have left. At the Queen Elizabeth Park in Uganda near Murchison falls – there were over 200 lions before lockdown, now there are only 70 and the two pride males have each lost a leg in a snare. In South Africa Pit track – a canine unit that works in the greater Kruger National Park managed to stop a lot of rhino poaching and a ranger in Botswana known as poster won an award for his work saving rhino’s there. ( The Joubert’s have footage we can use of some of these projects and are in contact with rangers across the continent. They also have some interviews done which we can use.)

As Derek Joubert tells Carte Blanche, for the first time we stopped focusing on the wildlife and looked at the critical role that rangers play in guarding the crown jewels of Africa, the animals that attract international dollars.

Says Joubert: “Our philosophy – for anything to succeed, we need to look down and we need to look at the horizon and protect these wild places. If we don’t look down right now there won’t be an horizon. There won’t be these parks to rebuild that 50 billion dollar income stream. It’s a spotlight on why rangers are so important. The time has come for rangers to get their own profile and the only way to get there is to let rangers and people know that they are appreciated. If we are in any way going to achieve 30% of the planet protected by 2030, which is a global goa,l we need to protect what we have right now, then the world’s attention needs to focus on the rangers.”

The Joubert’s had government officials phoning them asking for help as the tourism dollars dried up. So they decided to do something and have set up a project to try and fund as many rangers as they can across the continent.

“It’s a bit like a bandage on a gaping wound” says Beverly Joubert, ‘but we had to do something’.

So far they have managed to fund about 109 ranger salaries and already in places like Tanzania they are seeing some successes. But its an uphill battle.

Carte Blanche speaks to the Joubert’s, rangers, Chris Galyards, the president of the international ranger federation and follows rangers like Carl Thornton of Pit track to raise awareness of the dire straits that has beset African wildlife.

FINAL SCRIPT POACHING PANDEMIC for TX 5th December 2021

Commentary One
Its close to 42 degrees in the greater Kruger national Park and Carl Thornton and his rangers have embarked on an exercise- This is their life. Just add adrenaline

Carl Thornton over patrol
We are under full blown attack here, there’s no joke. It’s an incursion every second day.

Carl shouts to dog!

Carl
Multiple groups, groups coming out of Mozambique following the Oliphants river down, attacking us from the north. We have groups of poachers coming down south from Kruger National park, we are getting attacked from our east. Groups of SA poachers coming out of Phalaborwa. At any given time in KNP you are looking at 30 syndicates of three to four people running around 24/7

DEREK LINK
The natural assets of many African countries are facing an onslaught of organized crime, and its often tiny teams of rangers acting more like soldiers than guardians of nature who are left holding the line

Commentary two
21 years ago Carl Thornton gave up his job and started a small NGO called Pit- track.

Up sound ranger Olga “Leave elly”

Today this canine unit has 20 dogs that protect a reserve, a rhino orphanage and the entry and exits of the Timbavati - bordering Kruger National Park

Up sound Dog barks.

If you are bringing in weapons or smuggling out rhino horn, ivory or pangolin, these dogs and their handlers will probably catch you.

Carl
The easiest way to poach a rhino was just to drive in with a vehicle, shoot the rhino out the car window, chop its horn off, put in a car and drive out the front gate. It’s a whole lot easier than walking on foot from Mozambique, this is how brazen it was, this is exactly what was happening.

Commentary three
Their presence at these gates has seen at least a 70% reduction in syndicate poaching, but despite multiple interventions, the Rhino in the greater Kruger may not survive


Carl
I have been 21 years in the bush protecting animals. Look at the Kruger National Park. They lost 75% of their rhino’s. 260 black rhino’s. We’ll see extinction of black rhino’s in the wild in the next five years.

Commentary four
But it’s not just animals we are losing, in this war to save our wildlife the rangers themselves often pay the ultimate price.

DEREK LINK
It’s absolutely shocking when you look at this long list of rangers that have died in the line of duty across Africa. Some killed by the animals they were protecting, but many -just murdered

Commentary five
Chris Galliers is the president of the international ranger federation – a global body that represents over 100 ranger associations. They keep a tally of ranger deaths

Chris Galliers
Over the last 10 years we have lost 1200 rangers globally and many are due to homicides. These people are putting their lives on the line and getting killed to secure the natural heritage of future generations and they need all the support they can get

Commentary Six
At the recent COP 26 conference, this global federation called for rangers to be considered essential workers

Derek
And all the talks in Glasgow at the Cop conference, do they really help?
Chris
A lot of the talks are put into plans that are long term plans. We don’t have that time. We need the changes now and I think what is important is that those people at those conferences understand exactly what it is like to be on the ground out in the field, defending nature and ensuring it’s going to be here for eternity.

Commentary seven
On the ground it’s dangerous. In the KZN town of Hluhluwe is Project Rhino- an NGO that now targets all wildlife crime, and then some

Up sound: JUST MOVE ALONG!

They work closely with the Hawks, the SAPS and various security companies.

Photo clicks up sound

But barely a day goes by when they aren’t facing down one or other criminal syndicate.

Up sound ranger war cry -

Ranger Project Rhino
We are dealing with meat poachers, rhino poachers. There’s theft, there’s human trafficking, car hijackers- we are dealing with all of those things

Up sound patrol

Ranger man
We are dealing with well-trained guys who are doing these things.

Up sound plane starts

Ranger Project Rhino
We can say we are winning but we are not winning. It’s a 50/50. If a suspect is arrested today our government is not doing good, cos you can arrest someone, two or three days he is out there then this thing carries on and on. You can win today, but tomorrow you have to go and chase the very same guy-that means it’s three steps forward, five steps back. Then You have to keep on fighting, fighting, fighting

Up sound catching poachers and plane overhead

Ranger Project Rhino
We are making a difference but in a reserve maybe we have to do some patrols, we can take out maybe 25- 30 snares, just one trip. Imagine if those snares are there for two or three days- How many animals are we going to lose?

Derek Joubert
When we were born there were 450 000 lions. Today there are not even 20 000 lions.
This is a race against time and we are losing that race.

Commentary eight
Wild life film makers Derek and Beverley Joubert have spent more than two decades documenting Africa’s wildlife

Today they are National Geographic conservationists in residence in Botswana.

Their films, once a celebration of nature – now carry an urgent message – save Africa’s wildlife.

Music up sound over wildlife

Derek
We have seen massive 90% declines in wildlife across the board.



Commentary nine
Their voice has influence in high places, and that’s set them on a collision course against powerful trafficking and poaching syndicates.

Derek Joubert
This is at an industrial scale, this is multinational highly organised crime.
DW
Do you ever feel your lives are in danger?
Derek Joubert
Yes we get death threats all the time. All the time. Once a week!
Beverley
And it could be to frighten us away from the situation..
Derek Joubert
And so we have become fairly callous to those. And sometimes we even put them into categories of casual death threat, more serious death threat or bad death threat! laughs. But we know what we are doing and why we are doing it, and we won’t waiver, this is our mission.

Commentary ten
And with scientists predicting up to a million species on track for extinction in the coming decades, could that mission be any more critical

Derek Link
Then came Covid, the world locked down and tourism came to a grinding halt

Commentary eleven
Rangers were furloughed and across Africa, animals, already in a precarious position, lost many of their protectors

Beverley
In 2019 there was a 39 billion dollar tourist industry coming into the whole of Africa.
2020- 2021 that went down to pretty much zero. And many of the 40 000 anti-poaching units and rangers were furloughed
Derek
The level of laying off rangers, was catastrophic!

Commentary twelve
And the Joubert’s suddenly found themselves with 700 staff at their camps across the continent, and no guests. They decided they would cut costs, not staff, and the game under their custodianship, would have protectors, no matter what.

Derek Joubert
March last year looked left right and realized that there was going to be a poaching pandemic. Looked at our staff and said who can drive, who can be out in the field? So I redeployed everybody into anti-poaching duties. And so then we started to look at who else needed help, and everybody needed help!

Commentary thirteen
From Bumi Hills in Zimbabwe – across to Conservation lower Zambezi in Zambia, in the DRC, Uganda, Tanzania – private and state rangers were on their knees – salaries and supplies dried up - Gorillas, giraffe, lions, elephants- it was open season for anyone

Carl
If you look at Tshokwane in KNP they lost 14 rhino’s in 12 days.

Commentary fourteen
At first Carl Thornton thought that Pit Track may have to retrench almost all his rangers

Carl
It was a difficult time. These international tourists pay a conservation levy and that pays anti-poaching units

Commentary fifteen
It was a picture mirrored across the continent. Suddenly the Joubert’s realized that saving rangers was as important as saving a species and they started project ranger – a drive to raise funds to support salaries and supplies. That’s helped keep rangers in the field in 9 African countries

In Tanzania for example that’s helping save the giraffe

Derek
They had to furlough half of their anti-poaching force. We got them back in again within 6 days. There was a massive wave of giraffe snaring, just in the six days they were out of action

Commentary sixteen
Project rhino and Pit Track both received vital funds

Carl Thornton
Project ranger was a life saver. If it wasn’t for project ranger – there would be nothing in these reserves to protect.

Commentary seventeen
And even as tourism slowly returns, it’s clear that rangers across Africa need far more support. Sometimes it’s just a jerry can of fuel or a mosquito net, or rations for a long patrol. So it looks like project ranger is here to stay.

Derek
One of the things I worry about is that we will all rush back to normality and I think that we shouldn’t. I think we have had the most extraordinary opportunity to redraw our contract with nature. There was a moment in time where the skies had no aero planes in them, where wildlife was running down the city streets of new York, we should learn from that and try and understand and redefine how we want to have the perfect canvas now that it’s been blank.
Derek Watts
Because we had expanded our boundaries in a way?
Derek Joubert
Totally. We are encouraging people to be introspective and think about this moment and then to renew your vows with nature. This is our time

THE END 11 00

PROMO ONE 11 seconds
The Covid Pandemic decimated African tourism, leaving thousands of rangers furloughed, and the wildlife they protected at the mercy of international syndicates

PROMO TWO 21 seconds

Commentary
Its low paid, dangerous work. Rangers across Africa face multiple threats every day

Ranger Project Rhino
We are dealing with meat poachers, rhino poachers. There’s theft, there’s human trafficking, car hijackers- we are dealing with all of those things

Commentary
Carte Blanche joins rangers on the front lines

Plane overhead up sound


PROMO THREE
Game Rangers are having to act more like soldiers to protect Africa’s last remaining wildlife

Carl
We have groups of poachers coming down south from Kruger National park, we are getting attacked from our east. We under full blown attack here

Commentary
As a million species are on track for extinction, Game rangers are fighting international wildlife syndicates in a race against time.

And sometimes we even put them into categories of casual death threat, more serious death threat or bad death threat! laughs. But we know what we are doing and why we are doing it, and we won’t waiver, this is our mission. Commentary ten And with scientists predicting up to a million species on track for extinction in the coming decades, could that mission be any more critical Derek Link Then came Covid, the world locked down and tourism came to a grinding halt Commentary eleven Rangers were furloughed and across Africa, animals, already in a precarious position, lost many of their protectors Beverley In 2019 there was a 39 billion dollar tourist industry coming into the whole of Africa. 2020- 2021 that went down to pretty much zero. And many of the 40 000 anti-poaching units and rangers were furloughed Derek The level of laying off rangers, was catastrophic! Commentary twelve And the Joubert’s suddenly found themselves with 700 staff at their camps across the continent, and no guests. They decided they would cut costs, not staff, and the game under their custodianship, would have protectors, no matter what. Derek Joubert March last year looked left right and realized that there was going to be a poaching pandemic. Looked at our staff and said who can drive, who can be out in the field? So I redeployed everybody into anti-poaching duties. And so then we started to look at who else needed help, and everybody needed help! Commentary thirteen From Bumi Hills in Zimbabwe – across to Conservation lower Zambezi in Zambia, in the DRC, Uganda, Tanzania – private and state rangers were on their knees – salaries and supplies dried up - Gorillas, giraffe, lions, elephants- it was open season for anyone Carl If you look at Tshokwane in KNP they lost 14 rhino’s in 12 days. Commentary fourteen At first Carl Thornton thought that Pit Track may have to retrench almost all his rangers Carl It was a difficult time. These international tourists pay a conservation levy and that pays anti-poaching units Commentary fifteen It was a picture mirrored across the continent. Suddenly the Joubert’s realized that saving rangers was as important as saving a species and they started project ranger – a drive to raise funds to support salaries and supplies. That’s helped keep rangers in the field in 9 African countries In Tanzania for example that’s helping save the giraffe Derek They had to furlough half of their anti-poaching force. We got them back in again within 6 days. There was a massive wave of giraffe snaring, just in the six days they were out of action Commentary sixteen Project rhino and Pit Track both received vital funds Carl Thornton Project ranger was a life saver. If it wasn’t for project ranger – there would be nothing in these reserves to protect. Commentary seventeen And even as tourism slowly returns, it’s clear that rangers across Africa need far more support. Sometimes it’s just a jerry can of fuel or a mosquito net, or rations for a long patrol. So it looks like project ranger is here to stay. Derek One of the things I worry about is that we will all rush back to normality and I think that we shouldn’t. I think we have had the most extraordinary opportunity to redraw our contract with nature. There was a moment in time where the skies had no aero planes in them, where wildlife was running down the city streets of new York, we should learn from that and try and understand and redefine how we want to have the perfect canvas now that it’s been blank. Derek Watts Because we had expanded our boundaries in a way? Derek Joubert Totally. We are encouraging people to be introspective and think about this moment and then to renew your vows with nature. This is our time THE END 11 00 PROMO ONE 11 seconds The Covid Pandemic decimated African tourism, leaving thousands of rangers furloughed, and the wildlife they protected at the mercy of international syndicates PROMO TWO 21 seconds Commentary Its low paid, dangerous work. Rangers across Africa face multiple threats every day Ranger Project Rhino We are dealing with meat poachers, rhino poachers. There’s theft, there’s human trafficking, car hijackers- we are dealing with all of those things Commentary Carte Blanche joins rangers on the front lines Plane overhead up sound PROMO THREE Game Rangers are having to act more like soldiers to protect Africa’s last remaining wildlife Carl We have groups of poachers coming down south from Kruger National park, we are getting attacked from our east. We under full blown attack here Commentary As a million species are on track for extinction, Game rangers are fighting international wildlife syndicates in a race against time. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): African wildlife is in deep trouble as the global pandemic has led to another - a poaching pandemic
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Interviews with Derek and Beverly Joubert and unique footage from other african countries
metadata.Summary: In March last year when the world locked down, National Geographic conservationists Beverley and Derek Joubert looked around. They had 660 people working on their Great Plains Safari company in Botswana and absolutely no guests. The 50 billion dollars of revenue that comes into Africa and supports her wildlife dried up overnight and they knew that African wildlife was about to be in deep, deep trouble. Determined to try and keep their staff, the Joubert’s who have 1.2 million hectares under their custodianship -turned chefs and cooks into instant rangers and managed to keep their staff employed and most of their wildlife safe. But the Joubert’s have never been the kind of people to only consider their own needs, and driven by their imperative to conserve African wildlife, they asked how they could help. They spoke to conservationists across Africa, and to their network of wildlife investigators and realized another pandemic was taking place as rangers were furloughed, and organised trans national wildlife criminals moved into the vacuum left behind by the rangers. Says Derek Joubert: “The poaching that is taking place right now is not going to get meat locally – its organised transnational crime. If you consider that there are a billion containers moving around the ocean and about 10% of those have illegal wildlife products in them, so there is an entire industry around this, worth about 27 billion dollars. So the final point of this cycle is that wildlife is collapsing so we are into a second pandemic, a poaching pandemic. The world’s attention and certainly South Africa’s attention needs to focus on keeping rangers employed. It’s our collective duty, and if we don’t do anything, it’s our collective shame,” he says.
metadata.Further information: The examples the Joubert’s give, paint a grim picture. In Tanzania all the rangers were taken out of the field for 8 months leaving wildlife at the mercy of poachers. In Kenya the government is funding a survey that will soon go into the field to see how much wildlife they still have left. At the Queen Elizabeth Park in Uganda near Murchison falls – there were over 200 lions before lockdown, now there are only 70 and the two pride males have each lost a leg in a snare. In South Africa Pit track – a canine unit that works in the greater Kruger National Park managed to stop a lot of rhino poaching and a ranger in Botswana known as poster won an award for his work saving rhino’s there. ( The Joubert’s have footage we can use of some of these projects and are in contact with rangers across the continent. They also have some interviews done which we can use.) As Derek Joubert tells Carte Blanche, for the first time we stopped focusing on the wildlife and looked at the critical role that rangers play in guarding the crown jewels of Africa, the animals that attract international dollars. Says Joubert: “Our philosophy – for anything to succeed, we need to look down and we need to look at the horizon and protect these wild places. If we don’t look down right now there won’t be an horizon. There won’t be these parks to rebuild that 50 billion dollar income stream. It’s a spotlight on why rangers are so important. The time has come for rangers to get their own profile and the only way to get there is to let rangers and people know that they are appreciated. If we are in any way going to achieve 30% of the planet protected by 2030, which is a global goa,l we need to protect what we have right now, then the world’s attention needs to focus on the rangers.” The Joubert’s had government officials phoning them asking for help as the tourism dollars dried up. So they decided to do something and have set up a project to try and fund as many rangers as they can across the continent. “It’s a bit like a bandage on a gaping wound” says Beverly Joubert, ‘but we had to do something’. So far they have managed to fund about 109 ranger salaries and already in places like Tanzania they are seeing some successes. But its an uphill battle. Carte Blanche speaks to the Joubert’s, rangers, Chris Galyards, the president of the international ranger federation and follows rangers like Carl Thornton of Pit track to raise awareness of the dire straits that has beset African wildlife.
